answer:
A mobile pipeline is really two pipelines — a fast lane that must finish while the reviewer is still looking at the PR, and a slow lane that may take an hour — and most of the design work is deciding what belongs in which.

### Fast lane, on every PR
- **Lint and static analysis** — Detekt and ktlint on Android, SwiftLint and SwiftFormat on iOS, `dart analyze` for Flutter.
- Unit tests on the JVM or a simulator. No emulator, no signing, no uploads.

### Slow lane, on main or nightly
- Instrumented and UI tests on an emulator or simulator.
- Release builds, signed with material pulled from secrets.
- Artifact upload to TestFlight or Play internal testing for QA.
- Symbol upload (dSYMs, ProGuard mapping) so crash reports de-obfuscate.
- Staged rollout, driven by fastlane lanes or the store APIs.

Providers: GitHub Actions is the common default, with Bitrise and Codemagic as mobile-specialised options, plus CircleCI, Buildkite, and Xcode Cloud for iOS-only shops.

### Rules that keep it healthy
- Keep the PR build under about fifteen minutes, or people stop reading the results.
- Cache Gradle, SwiftPM and CocoaPods deliberately; an uncached mobile build is mostly downloading.
- Run everything you can on Linux runners. macOS runners cost several times more per minute, so reserve them for work that genuinely requires Xcode.
- Signing material never lives in the repository. It comes from encrypted secrets, is decoded at build time, and is never echoed into a log.
code_example:
# .github/workflows/android.yml — the fast PR lane
name: Android CI
on:
  pull_request: { branches: [main] }
  push: { branches: [main] }
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v5
        with: { distribution: 'zulu', java-version: '17' }
      - uses: gradle/actions/setup-gradle@v6      # caches, and validates the wrapper
      - run: ./gradlew detekt lintDebug
      - run: ./gradlew testDebugUnitTest
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v6
        if: failure()
        with: { name: test-reports, path: '**/build/reports/' }

  instrumented:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest      # KVM on Linux is faster AND far cheaper than a macOS runner
    needs: test
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - name: Enable KVM
        run: |
          echo 'KERNEL=="kvm", GROUP="kvm", MODE="0666", OPTIONS+="static_node=kvm"' \
            | sudo tee /etc/udev/rules.d/99-kvm4all.rules
          sudo udevadm control --reload-rules && sudo udevadm trigger --name-match=kvm
      - uses: reactivecircus/android-emulator-runner@v2
        with:
          api-level: 36
          script: ./gradlew connectedDebugAndroidTest

# .github/workflows/ios.yml — macOS runners only where Xcode is unavoidable
# jobs:
#   test:
#     runs-on: macos-latest
#     steps:
#       - uses: actions/checkout@v6
#       - run: bundle exec fastlane scan --device "iPhone 17"

answer:
Fastlane is a Ruby toolkit that turns the release ritual — build, sign, upload symbols, ship to a test track — into named lanes you run identically on a laptop and in CI.

### Common automations
- **Build and sign** — `build_app` (formerly `gym`) on iOS, the `gradle` action on Android.
- **Code signing** — `match` synchronises iOS certificates and provisioning profiles through a private, encrypted git repository (or S3, or Google Cloud Storage).
- **Store authentication** — `app_store_connect_api_key` loads an App Store Connect API key from an issuer id, key id and private key file. This is what CI should use; an Apple ID with an app-specific password is the legacy path and breaks on 2FA challenges.
- **Beta distribution** — `upload_to_testflight`, `firebase_app_distribution`, `upload_to_play_store` on the internal track.
- **Production** — `deliver` for the App Store, `supply` for Play, both scriptable including staged rollout percentages.
- **Screenshots** — `snapshot` drives UI tests across locales and devices, `frameit` decorates them, `deliver` uploads them.
- **Symbols** — `upload_symbols_to_crashlytics` and the Sentry plugin, so release crash reports are readable.

Why it survives: the same lane runs on a laptop and on CI, so 'works on my machine' becomes a testable claim. The alternative is a pile of bash that only one person understands, and that person is on holiday during the release.
code_example:
# fastlane/Fastfile — Android
default_platform(:android)

platform :android do
  desc "Build and upload to Play internal testing"
  lane :internal do
    gradle(task: "clean bundleRelease")
    upload_to_play_store(
      track: "internal",
      release_status: "draft",
      aab: "app/build/outputs/bundle/release/app-release.aab",
      mapping_paths: ["app/build/outputs/mapping/release/mapping.txt"]
    )
  end
end

# fastlane/Fastfile — iOS
platform :ios do
  desc "Build and upload to TestFlight"
  lane :beta do
    setup_ci if is_ci                      # keychain the runner can actually use

    # API key, not an Apple ID: unattended, and immune to 2FA prompts
    api_key = app_store_connect_api_key(
      key_id: ENV["ASC_KEY_ID"],
      issuer_id: ENV["ASC_ISSUER_ID"],
      key_content: ENV["ASC_KEY_P8"]
    )

    match(type: "appstore", readonly: is_ci, api_key: api_key)
    increment_build_number(xcodeproj: "MyApp.xcodeproj")
    build_app(scheme: "MyApp", export_method: "app-store-connect")
    upload_to_testflight(api_key: api_key, skip_waiting_for_build_processing: true)
    upload_symbols_to_crashlytics(gsp_path: "./MyApp/GoogleService-Info.plist")
  end
end

# In CI
# bundle exec fastlane android internal
# bundle exec fastlane ios beta

answer:
iOS signing is four moving parts that all have to agree: a certificate identifying who built the binary, a provisioning profile binding an App ID to that certificate, entitlements compiled into the app, and a bundle identifier that already exists in App Store Connect.

### Getting the material onto CI
- `fastlane match` stores certificates and profiles in a private repository, encrypted with a passphrase. CI clones and installs them in read-only mode, so a runner can never regenerate and thereby revoke the whole team's certificates.
- Authenticate with an App Store Connect API key rather than an Apple ID — two-factor authentication makes password auth unusable unattended.
- Xcode Cloud, or Xcode's automatic signing, is a reasonable choice for a small team that does not need the pipeline reproducible anywhere else.

### Distribution paths
- **TestFlight** — up to 100 internal testers with no review, up to 10 000 external testers behind a lighter review.
- **App Store** — full review, then either an immediate release or a phased rollout.
- Ad hoc and enterprise in-house distribution still exist but are narrow and increasingly legacy.

### Gotchas that actually bite
- Regenerating a profile can silently drop capabilities such as push or App Groups, and entitlements in the binary must match the profile exactly. That mismatch is caught at upload processing, not at build time, so it fails after the slow part.
- Apple raises the minimum build SDK every year; the current cycle requires uploads built with Xcode 26 and the iOS 26 SDK. Check the deadline before planning a release freeze, and do not confuse the build SDK with your deployment target.
- An expired certificate does not break installed apps, only new builds — so the failure always turns up on a deadline.
code_example:
# One-time setup, run by a human on a Mac
fastlane match init
fastlane match appstore              # creates or fetches cert + profile, encrypted into the repo

# CI: read-only, so a runner can never revoke the team's certificates
export MATCH_PASSWORD="${MATCH_PASSWORD}"
bundle exec fastlane match appstore --readonly

# Archive and export with explicit signing
xcodebuild -workspace MyApp.xcworkspace -scheme MyApp \
  -configuration Release -archivePath build/MyApp.xcarchive archive \
  CODE_SIGN_STYLE=Manual \
  PROVISIONING_PROFILE_SPECIFIER="match AppStore com.example.app" \
  CODE_SIGN_IDENTITY="Apple Distribution"

xcodebuild -exportArchive \
  -archivePath build/MyApp.xcarchive \
  -exportPath build \
  -exportOptionsPlist ExportOptions.plist

# Upload with an API key — no Apple ID, no 2FA prompt on a headless runner
bundle exec fastlane pilot upload --ipa build/MyApp.ipa

# ExportOptions.plist
# <key>method</key><string>app-store-connect</string>   <- 'app-store' is the old spelling
# <key>signingStyle</key><string>manual</string>
# <key>uploadSymbols</key><true/>

# Matchfile — note there is no username; auth comes from the API key
# git_url("git@github.com:org/certs.git")
# storage_mode("git")
# type("appstore")
# app_identifier(["com.example.app"])

# fastlane match nuke appstore    # revokes everything. Never from CI.

answer:
Android has two signing keys and the important one is not yours: you sign with an upload key, and Play App Signing re-signs the artifact with the app signing key that devices actually verify.

- **Upload key** — signs the AAB you upload. If you lose it, Play can reset it, which is the entire reason Play App Signing is worth using.
- **App signing key** — held by Google, used to sign the APKs delivered to devices.
- **Build types**: `debug` uses the shared debug keystore, `release` uses your keystore injected from CI secrets.
- The AAB is the required upload format. Play splits it per device by ABI, density and language, so what installs is never quite what you built — use `bundletool` when you need to reproduce a device's actual APK locally.

### Distribution tracks
- **Internal testing** — up to 100 testers, no review wait. This is where CI should push on every main-branch build.
- **Closed and open testing** — larger audiences, still reviewed.
- Production, with a staged rollout percentage you control and can halt.

### Policy gates that block a release
- Target API level, which Play raises annually. From 31 August 2026, new apps and updates must target Android 16 (API level 36), while existing apps need at least API level 35 to stay available to new users.
- A completed Data safety form and a privacy policy.
- 64-bit native libraries.
- An in-app account deletion path for apps with sign-in.

Keystore handling: base64 it into a CI secret, decode into the workspace at build time, delete it afterwards, and never echo the passwords into the log. Gradle will happily print them if you interpolate them into a task name.

Flavors let you produce multiple APKs/AABs from one codebase, differing in package name, branding, endpoints, or features.

### Android (Gradle)
- `productFlavors { free { ... }; paid { ... } }`
- Combined with `buildTypes { debug; release }` to give variants like `freeDebug`, `paidRelease`.
- Each flavor can override resources, manifests, source sets.

### iOS (Xcode)
- **Multiple targets** — separate builds, separate Info.plist.
- Or schemes + xcconfig files — single target, different config files for dev / staging / prod.
- Asset catalogues + Info.plist substitution for branding.

### Flutter
- `--flavor` flag with `--dart-define` for compile-time constants.

### Use flavors for
- Dev / staging / prod with different API endpoints.
- White-label apps (same codebase, multiple branded apps).
- Free vs paid SKUs.
- Feature subsets per geography.

Keep flavor count small; each one multiplies your CI build matrix.

Staged rollout = release to a small percent first, watch metrics, ramp.

### Android (Play Console)
- Production → Releases → set rollout percentage (1%, 5%, 20%, 50%, 100%).
- Halt rollout if vitals drop. Resume when fixed (the affected version stays at the lower %).
- **Internal app sharing** — quick QA URLs.

### iOS (App Store)
- Phased release for automatic updates: 1%, 2%, 5%, 10%, 20%, 50%, 100% over 7 days.
- Manual users get the app immediately.
- Pause / resume at any stage.
- Expedited review for critical fixes (use sparingly).

### Observability during rollout
- **Crash-free users** — Crashlytics / Sentry.
- ANR rate (Android) — Play Vitals.
- **Frame rate / startup** — Firebase Performance / MetricKit.
- **Funnel + business metrics** — Mixpanel / Amplitude.
- **Server logs** — error rate, latency.

Playbook: define KPIs and thresholds BEFORE shipping. Wire alerts (PagerDuty / Slack). Have a rollback plan: feature flags first, app pull-from-store as last resort.
code_example:
# fastlane — staged Play rollout
lane :production_5pct do
  upload_to_play_store(
    track: "production",
    rollout: "0.05",                 # 5%
    aab: "app/build/outputs/bundle/release/app-release.aab"
  )
end

lane :production_50pct do
  upload_to_play_store(
    track: "production",
    rollout: "0.5",
    skip_upload_apk: true,            # already uploaded
    skip_upload_aab: true
  )
end

# Halting via Play Console UI is recommended — fastlane can change rollout but the UI is faster in incidents.

# iOS phased release — toggle in App Store Connect:
# 'Phased Release for Automatic Updates' = ON

# Observability dashboard — track these on a per-version basis:
# - crash-free users (target > 99.5%)
# - ANR rate (target < 0.5%)
# - p99 cold startup (target < 2s)
# - business KPI: signup conversion, checkout success rate

# Rollback decision tree
# 1. Crash spike from new code path -> flip feature flag OFF
# 2. Cannot mitigate via flag -> halt rollout, ship hotfix in next update
# 3. Severe regression -> Play 'halt rollout' / iOS 'pause phased release', expedited review

answer:
Measure before you optimise, because the wall clock in a mobile pipeline is usually dependency resolution, an emulator boot, or a job that never needed to run at all. A Gradle build scan or Xcode's build timing summary tells you which, and guessing usually picks the wrong one.

### Stop doing work nobody asked for
- A concurrency group keyed on the branch with cancel-in-progress kills the run that a new push has already superseded. On a busy repository this is the single cheapest saving available.
- Path filters or affected-module detection so a change to the README does not build two apps.
- Debug builds on PRs, release builds on main. Coverage instrumentation, screenshot generation and the full device matrix belong in the nightly lane.

### Cache deliberately
- Key caches on the lockfile hash and give them a fallback prefix, so a dependency bump degrades to a partial hit instead of a cold build.
- Cache the Gradle user home, the resolved SwiftPM packages, CocoaPods and the Ruby bundle. Do not cache DerivedData wholesale — a stale one produces failures nobody can reproduce, and the hour you lose debugging that erases a week of savings.
- Turn on Gradle's configuration cache and build cache, and share the build cache remotely so CI and laptops warm each other. Do not run `clean` out of superstition; bust the cache key when you genuinely need a cold build.

### Split rather than lengthen
- Shard the test suite across parallel runners. Ten minutes of tests on six runners is a two-minute job.
- Enable parallel testing in Xcode and raise Gradle's parallel forks, and let independent jobs run concurrently instead of forming one long chain.

### Spend the money where it works
- Anything that does not need Xcode belongs on a Linux runner, because a macOS minute costs several times as much.
- Emulator boot dominates instrumented runs. Gradle Managed Devices with an automated-test-device image, plus hardware acceleration on Linux, take minutes off every run.
- A larger runner is often the same total cost for half the wall clock, and it returns those minutes to every reviewer.
- Prebuild heavy, rarely-changing dependencies into binary frameworks instead of compiling them on every run.

Then watch the trend rather than one build. Publish job duration to a dashboard: a pipeline that rots by ten seconds a week is exactly how it reached forty minutes without anyone noticing.
code_example:
# .github/workflows/pr.yml — the levers that actually move the number
name: PR
on: pull_request
concurrency:
  group: pr-${{ github.ref }}      # a new push cancels the run it superseded
  cancel-in-progress: true
jobs:
  changes:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      android: ${{ steps.filter.outputs.android }}
      ios: ${{ steps.filter.outputs.ios }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - uses: dorny/paths-filter@v3
        id: filter
        with:
          filters: |
            android: ['android/**', 'shared/**', 'gradle/**']
            ios: ['ios/**', 'shared/**']

  android:
    needs: changes
    if: needs.changes.outputs.android == 'true'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest          # Linux minutes are a fraction of macOS minutes
    strategy:
      matrix: { shard: [0, 1, 2, 3] }   # split the suite, do not lengthen the job
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v5
        with: { distribution: zulu, java-version: '17' }
      - uses: gradle/actions/setup-gradle@v6
      - run: ./gradlew testDebugUnitTest -Pshard=${{ matrix.shard }} -Pshards=4
        env:
          GRADLE_OPTS: >-
            -Dorg.gradle.configuration-cache=true
            -Dorg.gradle.caching=true
            -Dorg.gradle.parallel=true

  ios:
    needs: changes
    if: needs.changes.outputs.ios == 'true'
    runs-on: macos-15               # only where Xcode is genuinely unavoidable
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData/**/SourcePackages
          key: spm-${{ hashFiles('**/Package.resolved') }}
          restore-keys: spm-        # a partial hit still beats a cold resolve
      - run: |
          xcodebuild test -scheme MyApp -parallel-testing-enabled YES \
            -destination 'platform=iOS Simulator,name=iPhone 17'

# Deliberately absent: a whole-DerivedData cache. Stale contents produce failures
# nobody can reproduce, and one of those costs more than the caching ever saved.

answer:
Secrets have to be unreachable from any code a stranger can change, which mostly means fork pull requests run without them and release jobs sit behind a human approval.

### The traps, in the order they bite
- Fork pull requests get no secrets on the ordinary trigger, which is the safe default. `pull_request_target` is the hole — it runs in the base branch's context with secrets and write scope, so a workflow that then checks out the pull request's head and runs its build is handing an attacker everything. If you need that trigger, check out the base only, or split into an untrusted build job and a trusted job that consumes its artifact.
- A build script is code. A pull request that edits a Gradle file, a Gradle plugin, the Gemfile, the Podfile or a fastlane action runs on your runner before any human reviews the diff. Review dependency changes as carefully as source, and keep checksummed lockfiles.
- Third-party actions pinned to a tag can be moved under you. Pin to a full commit SHA; that is precisely how several supply-chain incidents worked.

### The controls worth having
- Set explicit least-privilege permissions on the workflow token. The default grant is wider than any build needs.
- Put real secrets in a protected environment with required reviewers, so publishing to TestFlight or Play needs a person and an ordinary CI job cannot read the signing material at all.
- Prefer short-lived credentials from OIDC federation over long-lived cloud access keys — nothing to leak, nothing to rotate.
- Keep `fastlane match` in read-only mode on CI, so a compromised or merely confused runner can never revoke and regenerate the team's certificates.
- Self-hosted runners must be ephemeral and must never accept fork pull requests. A persistent runner keeps whatever the previous job left behind, including a poisoned cache.
- Log masking is not a control. Base64 or a split string defeats it, so enable secret scanning and push protection, and treat any secret that reached a log as burned and rotate it.

The useful mental model: assume every job that builds untrusted code is already compromised, and design so that job has nothing worth taking.
code_example:
# A fork PR builds with no secrets present. Keep it that way.
name: CI
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]
permissions:
  contents: read           # least privilege; the default token grant is wider than this
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6      # in a real repo: pin to a full commit SHA
      - run: ./gradlew assembleDebug   # untrusted code runs here, so nothing secret is here

  release:
    if: github.event_name == 'push'
    needs: build
    runs-on: macos-15
    environment: production   # required reviewer; the signing secrets are scoped to it
    permissions:
      contents: read
      id-token: write         # OIDC gives short-lived cloud creds instead of stored keys
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/mobile-ci
          aws-region: eu-central-1
      - run: bundle exec fastlane ios beta      # match runs --readonly inside the lane
        env:
          MATCH_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.MATCH_PASSWORD }}

# ❌ the classic hole, in full
# on: pull_request_target                       # runs with secrets and write scope...
# jobs:
#   build:
#     steps:
#       - uses: actions/checkout@v6
#         with: { ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }} }   # ...checks out the PR...
#       - run: ./gradlew build                                       # ...runs their build script

answer:
Mobile releases are forward-only, so the branching model exists to make the ship date independent of whether any given feature is finished.

### The shape most teams converge on
- Trunk-based development. Short-lived branches into main, main always releasable, and unfinished work hidden behind a flag rather than parked on a branch. A three-week feature branch is a merge conflict with a deadline attached.
- Cut a release branch on the train's schedule. From that moment only fixes are cherry-picked onto it, main keeps moving, and the train leaves with whatever was on board.
- Tag what you shipped and build the store artifact from the tag. That tag is what a hotfix branches from three weeks later, when main has moved on by two hundred commits.
- Merge the hotfix back into main immediately, or you will ship the same bug again next train.

### Versioning that CI owns
- The release branch owns the marketing version; the build number comes from the CI run number so it is monotonic and never repeats. TestFlight rejects a duplicate build number and Play rejects a version code that is not higher, and both failures land after the slow part of the pipeline.
- Derive both from the pipeline. A human typing a version into a build file is a future release blocked at ten at night.

### What replaces rollback
- You cannot recall a build that is already installed. Halting a Play rollout or pausing a phased release only stops new users getting it.
- So the real rollback is a feature flag or a server-side switch, decided before the feature ships, and the kill switch is tested like any other code path.
- A forward hotfix takes as long as review takes, which is why the flag exists.

Process that keeps it boring: a named release owner, a written go or no-go with real criteria — crash-free rate on the previous version, blocking bugs, symbols uploaded, release notes translated — and a plan that respects the store's calendar as well as the sprint's, including review latency, seasonal freezes and the annual SDK deadline.
code_example:
# Cut the train on schedule; main keeps moving without you
git switch main && git pull
git switch -c release/8.4
git push -u origin release/8.4

# After the cut, only fixes ride the branch, and each one is an explicit cherry-pick
git switch release/8.4
git cherry-pick -x 9f2c1ab        # -x records the commit it came from
git push

# Ship from a tag, so a hotfix has something to branch from later
git tag -a v8.4.0 -m "8.4.0 (build 4213)"
git push origin v8.4.0

# Version numbers come from the pipeline, never from a human
# VERSION_CODE=$(( 10000 + GITHUB_RUN_NUMBER ))     # Play rejects a non-increasing one
# agvtool new-version -all "$GITHUB_RUN_NUMBER"     # TestFlight rejects a duplicate

# Hotfix: branch the tag, fix, ship, merge back or you reship the bug next train
git switch -c hotfix/8.4.1 v8.4.0
git cherry-pick -x 4ab77e0
git tag -a v8.4.1 -m "8.4.1"
git push origin hotfix/8.4.1 v8.4.1
git switch main && git merge --no-ff hotfix/8.4.1

# Nothing here recalls a build someone already installed.
# That is what the kill switch is for, and it ships before the feature does.
# curl -X POST "$FLAGS/api/flags/checkout-v2" -d '{"enabled": false}'

answer:
A crash report is only readable if the symbol file for that exact build was uploaded before anyone needed it, and rebuilding does not recreate it.

### What has to be produced and kept, per platform
- **iOS** — dSYM bundles, identified by a build UUID. The Release configuration must be set to produce them; a project that only generates them for Debug ships blind.
- **Android** — R8's mapping file for Java and Kotlin frames, and native debug symbols for anything in a shared library.
- **Flutter** — the split-debug-info output when you obfuscate, archived per version, because `flutter symbolize` needs the exact file.

The rule underneath all of it: compiler output is not bit-identical across machines and runs, so the mapping for build 4213 exists once. Upload it in the same job that produced the binary, and archive it next to the artifact for as long as that version is installed anywhere.

### iOS specifics
- App Store Connect reprocesses your upload and can produce its own dSYMs, so download them back after processing finishes and send those to your crash vendor. A missing one surfaces as a warning in the crash dashboard days later, when the crash you need is already unreadable.

### Android specifics
- Pass the mapping file to the Play upload so the console deobfuscates, and set the native debug symbol level so the bundle carries symbols for native frames.
- Play's console and your crash vendor do not share the file, so upload it to both.

### What makes it fail in practice
- A mismatch between the app's version and build number and the one attached to the symbol upload. The file is there, the stack is still hex, and nobody can see why.
- A manual step. The upload has to be part of the release lane, because the step that depends on somebody remembering is the step that gets skipped during an incident.
- Retention that only covers the current version. Old versions crash too, and they are precisely the ones you are trying to persuade people to upgrade from.
code_example:
# fastlane/Fastfile — symbols leave in the same lane that built the binary
platform :ios do
  lane :beta do
    api_key = app_store_connect_api_key(
      key_id: ENV["ASC_KEY_ID"],
      issuer_id: ENV["ASC_ISSUER_ID"],
      key_content: ENV["ASC_KEY_P8"]
    )
    build_app(scheme: "MyApp", export_method: "app-store-connect")
    upload_to_testflight(api_key: api_key)

    # Apple reprocesses the upload, so the authoritative dSYMs come back from App Store Connect
    download_dsyms(api_key: api_key, wait_for_dsym_processing: true)
    upload_symbols_to_crashlytics(gsp_path: "./MyApp/GoogleService-Info.plist")
    clean_build_artifacts
  end
end

platform :android do
  lane :internal do
    gradle(task: "bundleRelease")
    upload_to_play_store(
      track: "internal",
      mapping_paths: ["app/build/outputs/mapping/release/mapping.txt"]   # Play deobfuscates
    )
    gradle(task: "uploadCrashlyticsMappingFileRelease")   # and so does your crash vendor
    gradle(task: "uploadCrashlyticsSymbolFileRelease")    # native frames need their own upload
  end
end

# Build settings that must be right before any of this helps
# iOS:     DEBUG_INFORMATION_FORMAT = dwarf-with-dsym, on Release and not only on Debug
# Android: buildTypes { release { ndk { debugSymbolLevel = "FULL" } } }
#          firebaseCrashlytics { mappingFileUploadEnabled = true; nativeSymbolUploadEnabled = true }
# Flutter: flutter build ipa --obfuscate --split-debug-info=build/symbols/8.4.0
#
# Archive the symbols with the artifact. You cannot rebuild your way back to them.

answer:
Almost every unexplained CI failure comes from something nobody pinned — a runner image, a toolchain, or a dependency that resolved to a version which did not exist last week.

The usual sources, roughly in order of how often they bite:
- Runner images move. A `latest` macOS label changes which Xcode is default, and a `latest` Linux label changes the JDK and the NDK. Pin the image label, then select the toolchain explicitly inside it, and treat an image upgrade as a reviewed pull request.
- Xcode in particular is not just a compiler version. It changes the Swift language version, which simulator runtimes exist, and what the store will accept on upload, so pin it rather than trusting the default.
- Java, Gradle, the Android Gradle Plugin and Kotlin form a compatibility matrix. Commit the wrapper, validate it in CI, and declare a Java toolchain in the build so the runner's default JDK is not making the decision.
- Ruby and fastlane. Commit the lockfile and always run through `bundle exec`; a bare `fastlane` resolves to whatever the image happens to ship, which is the classic worked-yesterday failure.
- Floating dependency versions. A dynamic Gradle version, an unpinned CocoaPods entry or a Swift package tracking a branch turns somebody else's release into your outage. Commit the CocoaPods and Swift package lockfiles.
- Simulator and emulator images are versioned too, so pin the API level and the device — an Xcode image does not carry every older runtime.

### How to stay ahead of it rather than react
- Let a bot raise upgrades as pull requests, so a bump arrives with a green or red build attached and a person decides when to take it.
- Run a nightly canary on the floating `latest` images. It fails first, on nobody's deadline, instead of failing on every pull request the morning the image rolls out.
- Make the same versions reproducible locally with a tool-version file or a dev container, so the person debugging is not also fighting their own machine.

The underlying principle is that a build is only reproducible if every input is a version you chose. Anything you left to a default is a change scheduled by someone else.
code_example:
# Pin the image, then pin the toolchain inside it
jobs:
  ios:
    runs-on: macos-15          # not macos-latest: the default Xcode moves under you
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - uses: maxim-lobanov/setup-xcode@v1
        with: { xcode-version: '26.0' }
      - uses: ruby/setup-ruby@v1
        with: { bundler-cache: true }          # resolves from Gemfile.lock
      - run: |
          xcodebuild test -scheme MyApp \
            -destination 'platform=iOS Simulator,name=iPhone 17,OS=26.0'
      - run: bundle exec fastlane ios beta     # never a bare `fastlane`

  android:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v5
        with: { distribution: zulu, java-version: '17' }   # not whatever the image ships
      - uses: gradle/actions/wrapper-validation@v6         # supply-chain and drift check in one
      - run: ./gradlew assembleDebug

  canary:
    if: github.event_name == 'schedule'
    runs-on: macos-latest      # deliberately floating: it breaks here first, not on a PR
    continue-on-error: true
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - run: bundle exec fastlane ios test

# Committed, or the build is not reproducible:
#   Gemfile.lock, Podfile.lock, Package.resolved, gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties
#   .tool-versions (mise or asdf) so a laptop and the runner agree
#
# Banned in build files: a dynamic Gradle version such as '1.2.+' or 'latest.release',
# an unpinned pod, and a Swift package dependency tracking a branch.

A UI suite is only worth its runtime if a red build reliably means a broken app, and that is as much an infrastructure decision as a test-writing one.

### Where they run
- **Android** — emulators on Linux runners with hardware acceleration are the cheapest and fastest option. Gradle Managed Devices make the device a declared build input, so every run uses an identical image, and an automated-test-device image boots much faster because it ships without the Play Store and the usual system apps.
- **iOS** — simulators come free with the macOS runner you are already paying for, which is most of what a pull request needs.
- Real hardware earns its cost for what a simulator cannot show: manufacturer skins, biometric hardware, cameras, low-memory devices and vendor patches. Put a device farm on the nightly matrix rather than on every pull request.

What removes most flakiness before you write a single retry:
- Run with the test orchestrator and clear the package data between tests, so every test starts from a clean process and a clean app state.
- Disable animations on the device.
- Stub the network. A UI suite pointed at a staging backend measures the backend's uptime, not your app.
- Shard across parallel runners instead of letting the job get longer.

### A written flake policy is what keeps the signal
- Retry an individual failing test once automatically, and quarantine it out of the blocking suite if it fails again within the week, with an owner and a ticket.
- Never retry the whole job on failure. It hides the flake, doubles the bill, and teaches everyone to press rerun.
- Track flake rate per test as a real metric. A suite whose red builds are routinely ignored is worse than having no suite, because it costs money and buys nothing.

And collect the evidence automatically — video, device log, screenshots on failure and the test XML as artifacts — because a failure that only happens on the runner is debuggable only from what the runner kept. Split the suite by purpose too: a smoke run of the critical journeys on every pull request, the full matrix nightly and before every release cut.

The build number is pipeline state, not source a human edits: CI has to derive a value that only ever goes up.

- **iOS** has two fields. `CFBundleShortVersionString` is the marketing version users see (1.4.0); `CFBundleVersion` is the build number, which must be unique and increasing within one marketing version.
- **Android** has `versionName`, free text shown to users, and `versionCode`, an integer that must strictly increase and cannot exceed 2100000000.

### Where the number should come from
- Ask the store: `latest_testflight_build_number + 1` on iOS, the highest version code across all Play tracks + 1 on Android. Self-correcting, and immune to a branch that never merged.
- Or a monotonic counter you control — the CI run number, or `git rev-list --count HEAD`. Fine as long as it can never reset or go backwards.
- On modern Xcode projects the plist reads `$(MARKETING_VERSION)` and `$(CURRENT_PROJECT_VERSION)` from build settings, so editing Info.plist by hand changes nothing. `agvtool`, and fastlane's `increment_build_number` on top of it, writes the build setting.

### What burns a number permanently
- Deleting a TestFlight build or discarding a Play draft does not free its value. Play rejects a version code that was ever used in any track, including a closed test from a year ago.
- Two people bumping by hand on two branches collide at merge, and the collision only shows at upload — after the slow part of the pipeline.
- Internal app sharing on Play ignores version code ordering entirely, which is why it is the right channel for a quick QA build.

The split to keep in your head: the marketing version is a product decision that lives in git, the build number is a machine-generated fact that lives in the pipeline.
code_example:
# fastlane/Fastfile — the store is the source of truth for the next number
platform :ios do
  lane :beta do
    api_key = app_store_connect_api_key(
      key_id: ENV["ASC_KEY_ID"], issuer_id: ENV["ASC_ISSUER_ID"], key_content: ENV["ASC_KEY_P8"]
    )

    # Ask App Store Connect rather than trusting whatever is committed:
    # a branch that never merged cannot desync the counter this way.
    next_build = latest_testflight_build_number(api_key: api_key, version: get_version_number) + 1

    # Writes CURRENT_PROJECT_VERSION in the build settings via agvtool.
    # Editing Info.plist directly does nothing — the plist only holds $(CURRENT_PROJECT_VERSION).
    increment_build_number(build_number: next_build)

    build_app(scheme: "MyApp", export_method: "app-store-connect")
    upload_to_testflight(api_key: api_key)
  end
end

platform :android do
  lane :internal do
    codes = google_play_track_version_codes(track: "internal") +
            google_play_track_version_codes(track: "production")
    # A code used in ANY track is burned forever, so take the max across all of them.
    gradle(task: "bundleRelease", properties: { "versionCode" => codes.max.to_i + 1 })
    upload_to_play_store(track: "internal")
  end
end

# Marketing version: decided by people, committed to git.
# Build number: decided by the pipeline, never typed by a person.

The runner is almost always right: something the build needs is not in the repository, or has a different name once the filesystem stops being case-insensitive.

- **Untracked files the build reads** — `google-services.json`, `GoogleService-Info.plist`, an xcconfig holding keys, a `.env`. They are gitignored for good reasons, so the pipeline must write them from secrets and fail loudly when they are absent.
- **An over-broad ignore rule** — `*.jar` swallows `gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.jar`, `build/` swallows a source directory called `build`. `git check-ignore -v <path>` names the exact line to blame.
- **Case** — macOS is case-insensitive by default, the Linux runner is not, so an import with the wrong capitalisation compiles at home and fails in CI. Git also keeps the old spelling after a case-only rename unless you `git mv` through a temporary name.
- **The executable bit** — `gradlew` committed without `+x` fails with "Permission denied". Fix it with `git update-index --chmod=+x gradlew`.
- **Stale local state** — `~/.gradle`, DerivedData, a pod or a `mavenLocal()` artifact that only exists on your disk. You resolve from a cache, the runner resolves from the network.
- **Missing lockfiles** — `Podfile.lock`, `Package.resolved` and `Gemfile.lock` belong in git; without them the runner resolves different versions than you did.

### Reproducing it in thirty seconds
Clone the repo into a temporary directory and build there, or run `git clean -xdff` in place. Both give you what CI sees. A cheap guard for the pipeline is a step that fails when `git status --porcelain` is dirty after a build, which catches generated files somebody forgot to commit.

The rule underneath all of it: if the build needs a file, either the file is in git or the pipeline creates it. "It works on my machine" is a statement about your machine, not about the build.
code_example:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Reproduce the CI environment locally: a clean clone, nothing from your working copy.
set -euo pipefail

TMP="$(mktemp -d)"
git clone --depth 1 "file://$PWD" "$TMP/app"
cd "$TMP/app"

# 1. Files the build reads but git does not carry. CI must write these from secrets.
for f in android/app/google-services.json ios/Runner/GoogleService-Info.plist; do
  [ -f "$f" ] || echo "MISSING: $f — inject it from a CI secret, do not commit it"
done

# 2. Which ignore rule swallowed a file that should have been committed?
git check-ignore -v gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.jar || true   # a bare '*.jar' rule is the usual culprit

# 3. The executable bit is part of the tree; a missing one is "Permission denied" on the runner.
git ls-files -s gradlew    # want mode 100755, not 100644
# git update-index --chmod=+x gradlew

# 4. Case: macOS hides this, the Linux runner will not.
git ls-files | sort -f | uniq -di   # names differing only in case = a build that breaks on Linux

./gradlew --no-daemon assembleRelease

# In the pipeline, catch generated files nobody committed:
#   git status --porcelain | tee /dev/stderr | (! read)

A rebuild is a new binary — a different runner image, a dependency that resolved differently, a new build number — so what ships is not what anyone tested.

Compile once, in one job, and publish the `.ipa` or `.aab`, the symbol files and the resolved-version manifest as a single immutable artifact named by its build number. Every later stage moves that artifact; nothing recompiles.

- **iOS** — the TestFlight build *is* the App Store candidate. Submit the existing build number for review instead of uploading a fresh binary.
- **Android** — promote the same AAB between tracks by version code. The Play API takes a track promotion with no artifact attached.

### Where mobile differs from a server
- Configuration is compiled in, so you cannot promote a staging binary to production. The release candidate is built with production configuration from the start; flavors exist to give developers and QA a *separate* build, not to mutate the one you promote.
- Signing happens at build time, so the immutable artifact is a signed artifact. The only later re-signing is Play App Signing, which is Google's step and does not change what you shipped.

### The traps
- A deploy job that runs `build` again. That is the whole bug, and it hides because both builds usually work.
- Symbols separated from the binary. Archive the dSYMs and the R8 mapping with the artifact, keyed by version and build number, or the crash reports from this release are unreadable.
- Retention shorter than the release cycle — the default on hosted CI is often 90 days. A hotfix on a two-month-old release then has nothing left to promote, and you are back to rebuilding.

The mental model: CI produces one candidate, and every stage after it is metadata about that candidate.
code_example:
# Compile once; every later job only moves the artifact.
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: macos-15
    outputs:
      build-number: ${{ steps.rc.outputs.number }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - id: rc
        run: echo "number=$GITHUB_RUN_NUMBER" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
      - run: bundle exec fastlane ios build_rc build_number:$GITHUB_RUN_NUMBER
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: rc-${{ github.run_number }}
          path: |                       # binary AND symbols travel together
            build/MyApp.ipa
            build/MyApp.app.dSYM.zip
            build/versions.lock
          retention-days: 180           # longer than the release cycle, or a hotfix has nothing to promote

  testflight:
    needs: build
    runs-on: macos-15
    steps:
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with: { name: rc-${{ github.run_number }} }
      - run: bundle exec fastlane ios upload ipa:MyApp.ipa   # upload, never rebuild

  submit:
    needs: [build, testflight]
    environment: production            # a human approves; still no compiler runs here
    runs-on: macos-15
    steps:
      # iOS: submit the build TestFlight already has, by number.
      - run: |
          bundle exec fastlane run upload_to_app_store \
            build_number:${{ needs.build.outputs.build-number }} \
            skip_binary_upload:true submit_for_review:true
      # Android: promote the same AAB by version code — no artifact is attached.
      - run: |
          bundle exec fastlane run upload_to_play_store \
            track:internal track_promote_to:production \
            version_code:${{ needs.build.outputs.build-number }} \
            skip_upload_aab:true rollout:0.05

The private key's access control wants a UI confirmation that a headless session cannot display, so signing has to be given explicit non-interactive permission to use that key.

### What a headless signing session needs
1. **Its own keychain**, created per job. The login keychain of a shared runner is not it.
2. **Unlocked and in the search list** — `security unlock-keychain` plus `security list-keychains -d user -s`, or `codesign` will not even see the identity.
3. **A partition list** — after importing with `-T /usr/bin/codesign`, run `security set-key-partition-list -S apple-tool:,apple: -s -k <password>`. On modern macOS the `-T` flag alone is not enough; the partition list is what actually removes the prompt.
4. **No lock timeout** — `security set-keychain-settings -lut 21600`. The default relocks after a few minutes of inactivity, so a long archive dies halfway through with the same error.

fastlane packages all four: `setup_ci` creates a temporary keychain and `match --readonly` imports into it. Prefer that over hand-rolled `security` calls.

### What still bites after that
- Self-hosted runners accumulate keychains and duplicate identities, so `codesign` picks a valid but wrong one and the upload is rejected for the wrong team. Create an ephemeral keychain per job and delete it in a step that always runs.
- The same cause surfaces as `errSecInternalComponent` with no explanation at all. Check the partition list first.
- `-allowProvisioningUpdates` looks like the fix and is not: it needs App Store Connect credentials and lets a build machine mutate the team's profiles. Manual signing keeps CI a consumer of signing material, never a producer.

Rule of thumb: signing state on a runner should live and die with the job.
code_example:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# An ephemeral signing keychain: created, used, destroyed within one job.
set -euo pipefail

KEYCHAIN="$RUNNER_TEMP/build.keychain-db"
PASSWORD="$(uuidgen)"                      # nobody needs to know it; it dies with the job
trap 'security delete-keychain "$KEYCHAIN" || true' EXIT

security create-keychain -p "$PASSWORD" "$KEYCHAIN"
security set-keychain-settings -lut 21600 "$KEYCHAIN"   # do NOT let it relock mid-archive
security unlock-keychain -p "$PASSWORD" "$KEYCHAIN"
security list-keychains -d user -s "$KEYCHAIN" $(security list-keychains -d user | tr -d '"')

echo "$CERT_P12_BASE64" | base64 --decode > "$RUNNER_TEMP/cert.p12"
security import "$RUNNER_TEMP/cert.p12" -k "$KEYCHAIN" -P "$CERT_PASSWORD" \
  -T /usr/bin/codesign -T /usr/bin/security
rm -f "$RUNNER_TEMP/cert.p12"

# The step everyone forgets. Without it codesign prompts, and headless there is nobody to click.
security set-key-partition-list -S apple-tool:,apple: -s -k "$PASSWORD" "$KEYCHAIN" >/dev/null

security find-identity -v -p codesigning "$KEYCHAIN"    # exactly one identity, or you sign as the wrong team

xcodebuild -workspace MyApp.xcworkspace -scheme MyApp -configuration Release \
  -archivePath "$RUNNER_TEMP/MyApp.xcarchive" archive \
  CODE_SIGN_STYLE=Manual OTHER_CODE_SIGN_FLAGS="--keychain $KEYCHAIN"

# Equivalent in fastlane, and preferred:
#   setup_ci                      # temporary keychain, unlocked, partition list handled
#   match(type: "appstore", readonly: true)

Play re-signs your upload with the app signing key, so the certificate fingerprint on a user's device is Google's and not your upload key's — and every integration keyed to that fingerprint has to know both.

- OAuth clients, Maps and other restricted API keys, Firebase, Facebook key hashes and App Links all check the SHA-256 of the signing certificate. Copy the app signing key's fingerprint from the Play Console (Test and release → App integrity) and register it next to your upload and debug fingerprints.
- App Links fail silently rather than loudly: an `assetlinks.json` listing the wrong fingerprint produces no error, the link just opens in a browser instead of your app.

### The other half: the installed app is not your APK
- Play splits the AAB by ABI, screen density and language, so a device installs a base APK plus configuration splits. Sideloading only the base APK from an AAB crashes at startup because the required splits are missing.
- A density or locale you never exercised may simply not be installed on that device, and the resource lookup falls back quietly instead of failing where you would notice.

### How to test what users actually get
- **Internal app sharing** serves the real, Play-signed split set from a link, with no version code rules and no review wait. It is the fastest true reproduction of a production install.
- Locally, `bundletool build-apks --connected-device` followed by `install-apks` builds exactly the split set that device would receive, from the same AAB you are about to upload.

The rule: verifying a release means installing the artifact the store produces, not the artifact your build produced.
code_example:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# What you signed with (the upload key) — NOT what users verify.
keytool -list -v -alias upload -keystore upload.jks -storepass "$KEYSTORE_PASSWORD" | grep SHA256

# What users verify: Play re-signs with the app signing key.
# Play Console → Test and release → App integrity → App signing key certificate.
# Register THAT SHA-256 for the OAuth client, the Maps key restriction and assetlinks.json,
# or sign-in works locally and fails for every Play install.

# Build the exact split set a connected device would receive from this AAB.
bundletool build-apks \
  --bundle=app/build/outputs/bundle/release/app-release.aab \
  --output=app.apks --connected-device \
  --ks=upload.jks --ks-key-alias=upload --ks-pass="pass:$KEYSTORE_PASSWORD"

bundletool install-apks --apks=app.apks     # base + abi/density/language splits, like Play does

# Inspect what actually got signed and with which certificate:
unzip -p app.apks splits/base-master.apk > base.apk
apksigner verify --print-certs base.apk | grep 'SHA-256 digest'

# WRONG, and a classic support ticket:
#   unzip the AAB, install the base APK alone -> "app is missing required components"
#   (MissingSplitsException) because the configuration splits were never installed.

# Fastest production-faithful check: upload the AAB to Play internal app sharing and
# install from that link. No version code ordering, no review, real Play signing.

answer:
A successful upload only means App Store Connect accepted the bytes; processing, export compliance and Beta App Review all happen afterwards, and any of them can park the build silently.

### What happens after your lane exits
- **Processing** runs asynchronously and re-signs and thins the binary. Validation failures — a missing usage-description string, a missing or incomplete privacy manifest, an unsupported architecture — arrive as an email with an ITMS code long after the job reported success.
- **Export compliance** blocks distribution until a human answers the encryption question. Declare `ITSAppUsesNonExemptEncryption` in Info.plist and nobody has to.
- **Beta App Review** is required for the first build of a new version string when external testers are involved. Internal testers get it immediately.
- **Expiry** — a TestFlight build stops being installable 90 days after upload, which is usually why an old build "disappeared".

### Making the lane tell the truth
- `skip_waiting_for_build_processing: true` makes the job fast and its green meaningless. When the job's purpose is to deliver to testers, wait for processing so a validation failure fails the pipeline instead of an inbox.
- Play has the same shape of trap from the other side: a release that stays a draft because nothing published it, an upload rejected because an enabled language has no release notes, or the API refusing to send changes for review while another change is already pending.

The definition of done is "a tester can install it", so that is what the lane should assert. An upload step that exits zero is not a delivery.
code_example:
# fastlane/Fastfile — the lane is only green when a tester can actually install the build
platform :ios do
  lane :beta do
    api_key = app_store_connect_api_key(
      key_id: ENV["ASC_KEY_ID"], issuer_id: ENV["ASC_ISSUER_ID"], key_content: ENV["ASC_KEY_P8"]
    )
    build_app(scheme: "MyApp", export_method: "app-store-connect")

    upload_to_testflight(
      api_key: api_key,
      # Fast and dishonest: green here means "bytes accepted", and an ITMS validation
      # failure then arrives by email while everyone believes the build shipped.
      skip_waiting_for_build_processing: false,
      distribute_external: true,
      groups: ["QA"],                  # external groups need Beta App Review on a new version string
      changelog: File.read("../CHANGELOG_LATEST.md")
    )
  end
end

# Info.plist — answer export compliance declaratively so processing never waits on a person:
#   <key>ITSAppUsesNonExemptEncryption</key><false/>
# And ship PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy; a missing required-reason API entry is rejected at processing,
# not at build time.

platform :android do
  lane :internal do
    gradle(task: "bundleRelease")
    upload_to_play_store(
      track: "internal",
      release_status: "completed",     # not "draft", or it sits in the console doing nothing
      changes_not_sent_for_review: false
      # Release notes are required for every enabled language:
      # fastlane/metadata/android/en-US/changelogs/<versionCode>.txt
    )
  end
end

answer:
On iOS nearly everything, because Apple signs what users install; on Android it depends entirely on whether Google holds your app signing key.

### iOS
- Revoke the distribution certificate in the developer portal and reissue. Apps already on the App Store were re-signed by Apple, so installed apps are unaffected — only your own builds break until profiles are regenerated. `fastlane match nuke distribution` does the revoke-and-regenerate, after which every machine re-runs `match`.
- Ad hoc and in-house enterprise builds are the exception: those are validated against your certificate, so revoking it stops them installing and can stop them launching.
- Rotate the App Store Connect API key as well (Users and Access → Integrations). A `.p8` is a complete credential with no password behind it.

### Android
- **With Play App Signing**, the leaked key is only your upload key. Request an upload key reset in the Play Console, register the new certificate, and users notice nothing — Google's key never left Google.
- **Without it**, the leaked key is the app's identity. Anyone can build an update that devices will accept as yours by sideload, and you cannot change the key for existing installs. Signature scheme v3 key rotation only helps new installs on newer Android, so the real remedy is enrolling in Play App Signing before this happens, not after.
- Any Android key change invalidates every fingerprint-derived integration — OAuth clients, restricted API keys, App Links — so they all have to be re-registered.

Rotate the Play service account key too, or better, replace the key file with workload identity federation so there is nothing on a laptop to take.

The asymmetry worth remembering: an iOS app's identity is your Apple account, and an Android app's identity is a key you may still be holding yourself.
code_example:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# iOS — the certificate is replaceable because Apple signs what users install.
bundle exec fastlane match nuke distribution   # revoke certs + profiles for the whole team
bundle exec fastlane match appstore            # reissue, re-encrypt into the match repo
# CI then picks the new material up on its next run:
#   bundle exec fastlane match appstore --readonly
# Ad hoc / enterprise builds signed by the revoked cert stop installing — check what you distribute
# outside the store before pulling this lever.

# Rotate the App Store Connect API key: a .p8 has no password behind it.
# App Store Connect -> Users and Access -> Integrations -> revoke, then create, then update the secret.

# Android with Play App Signing: only the UPLOAD key leaked.
keytool -genkeypair -v -keystore upload-new.jks -alias upload -keyalg RSA -keysize 4096 -validity 10000
keytool -export -rfc -keystore upload-new.jks -alias upload -file upload-new.pem
# Play Console -> Test and release -> App integrity -> "Request upload key reset", attach upload-new.pem.
# The app signing key is untouched, so installed apps and their fingerprint stay valid.

# Every Android key change invalidates fingerprint-bound integrations. Re-register this:
keytool -list -v -keystore upload-new.jks -alias upload | grep SHA256

# Without Play App Signing there is no equivalent command, because there is no remedy:
# the leaked key IS the app's identity for every device that already installed it.
# apksigner rotate exists (signature scheme v3) but only protects new installs on newer Android.

answer:
Separate shipping from launching: get both binaries to users ahead of the date with the feature dark, then turn it on from the server once both are actually out.

### Why store dates cannot be the mechanism
- Review latency is not yours to control on either store, and both review production releases. Any plan whose critical path runs through review is a plan to slip.
- Even after approval, release is a curve, not a moment. Apple's phased release and Play's staged rollout mean the set of users holding the new binary on Tuesday is never all of them.

### The levers that do work
- **Hold approved builds.** App Store Connect's manual release and Play's managed publishing both park an approved release until you publish it. Get approved early, publish on your own schedule.
- **Gate the feature on a remote flag**, defaulting off, shipped in both binaries a release or two ahead. The flag is also your rollback, which matters because a build cannot be recalled.
- **Keep the backend serving the previous version** for as long as it is installed. The flag decides behaviour; the API cannot assume a client version.

### The traps
- Treating expedited review as a plan rather than an emergency lever. It is rationed, and spending it on a marketing date costs you the one time you will need it during an incident.
- A flag with no safe default. Cache the last known value and fall back to off when the config service is unreachable, or a launch day outage becomes a feature outage.
- Forcing an upgrade to align versions. It works and users hate it; keep it for security fixes.

The mental model: the store decides when the code is available, you decide when the feature is on.
code_example:
# Ship early and dark; launch later from the server.
name: release
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      publish: { description: 'publish approved builds now', type: boolean, default: false }

jobs:
  submit:
    runs-on: macos-15
    environment: production
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      # iOS: submit for review well before the date, then hold the approved build.
      - run: |
          bundle exec fastlane run upload_to_app_store \
            submit_for_review:true \
            automatic_release:false \
            phased_release:true          # you still choose the moment; Apple ramps from there
      # Android: managed publishing is enabled in the console, so an approved
      # release waits for you instead of going out the moment review clears.
      - run: |
          bundle exec fastlane run upload_to_play_store \
            track:production rollout:0.1 release_status:completed

  launch:
    needs: submit
    if: inputs.publish
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      # Both binaries are already on devices with the feature off. This is the launch.
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - run: |
          jq '.parameters.new_checkout.defaultValue.value = "true"' \
            remoteconfig.template.json > tmp && mv tmp remoteconfig.template.json
          firebase deploy --only remoteconfig
      # Same command with "false" is the rollback — seconds, not a new review cycle.
